Mr. Speaker, I should Tike to draw the attention 	.
of the government to a statement appearing in the press which has received wide publicity, and which casts an unfair reflection on the white producers of agricultural products in British Columbia. This despatch appears in our local papers and was sent from Vancouver on February 25 by the Canadian press:
Inability of white farmers of British Columbia to supply vegetables of quality available for shipment to China for consumption of troops stationed there, was given by R. G. L. Clarke, Dominion fruit inspector, here to-day, as the reason for their purchase from Chinese growers of the province. Twenty-five tons of potatoes and 14 tons of onions were shipped to the British authorities at Shanghai from here three weeks ago on the liner Empress of Asia, while ninety tons of potatoes and fifty tons of onions will be forwarded on the Empress of Canada which sails for China to-morrow. All of this produce is said to have been grown by orientals.
Mr. Clarke, who stated that he had purchased the supplies on behalf of the British government, said he was aware of their origin, but had been unable to secure other products of fit quality and that all his decisions in the matter had been approved by his superiors in Ottawa.
Protests against the alleged discrimination against whites have been forwarded to both the federal and provincial governments in Ottawa and Victoria by several Vancouver dealers.
This, Mr. Speaker, is a very serious and unfair reflection on our white growers of agricultural products in British Columbia. From years of experience out there I have found that they are capable of growing vegetables not only as well as but better than the orientals. I would ask the minister if he has any light to throw on the matter.

call the attention of the government to an item that appeared in the newspapers in Montreal on Saturday, to the effect that there would be an anti-rabies drive against all dogs found on the streets of that city. This is a very serious matter for all dog owners of Montreal inasmuch as they are unable to obtain the muzzles prescribed by the government officials. Furthermore, it is reported in the newspapers that the authorities have despatched inspectors and veterinaries, with the result that these dogs will be killed without the owners having any redresis. I would ask the minister in charge of this particular branch of government what the intention is in the matter, and to make some official statement in view of the fact that the public of Montreal have received no information except what appeared in the papers on Saturday.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
My hon. friend, I gather,
wants to know what we are going to do in regard to carrying out the muzzling order issued twelve months ago as a result of an outbreak of rabies in Montreal. The enforcement of this order is not easy in a city of such proportions. Dogs suffering from this affliction have been finding their way into other places and spreading the disease to such an extent that in some parts of the province of Quebec the situation is grave. Word has reached the foreign authorities and as a result the export of our foxes has suffered, one foreign country refusing to accept our live foxes. The time has come when we must enforce the regulation more strictly, especially as the provincial authorities of Quebec have drawn our attention to the fact that this has not been properly done so far. Instructions have been
given to the officers of my department to round up all unmuzzled or improperly muzzled dogs not on the leash, for the purpose of destroying them, of course in a humane way, under the auspices of the Humane Society. That order will be observed, I trust. It is the only way to eradicate the disease. . It took eight months to round up eight cases of rabies in the Ottawa district, and we have been at it twelve months in Montreal with the result that I have outlined; and unless we carry out the order more strictly, not only will the disease spread to other provinces, but it will affect human being3 as well. A hundred and forty cases of human rabies are being treated at the present time, and from the disease two deaths have so far resulted. It is therefore incumbent upon the department to carry out the order as rigidly as possible.

Mr. A. MacG. YOUNG (Saskatoon): There is a matter of great importance to our province which I desire to bring to the attention of the House this afternoon; but before doing so I desire to make a few observations with reference to some of the speeches already delivered in this debate. I take this early opportunity of saying, as one member of the House, that I regretted very much indeed the speech delivered the other evening by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Brady) so far as it had reference to the late member for that constituency, Mr. Stork. I came to this House last year a new member, unacquainted with that gentleman, but during my stay of six months here I got to know him better and I always found him in every way honourable. Indeed, I think I may safely say that every member of the last parliament found Mr. Stork an honourable member of the House. It was unfortunate, I think, that the present member for Mr. Stork's riding, in the sermon he delivered some days ago in this chamber, should have seen fit to suggest that his predecessor had been dishonest in his representation of his constituency in parliament, and

that he had not presented the facts to the House. I for one wish to place myself on record as being quite resentful of these remarks. It ill becomes any member of this honourable chamber to cast such aspersions upon a gentleman who enjoyed the confidence of those whom he represented here. Mr. Stork is not here to speak for himself, and when his opponent has already put him down it does not come with good grace from him to speak as he has done. I think perhaps if we were a little more careful in some of our imputations it would be better for the most of us. Referring now to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), I was very much surprised to hear him suggest that the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke) changed his seat from one side of the House to the other and entered the government apparently for a consideration of $14,000. Again I place myself on record as being most resentful of that sort of imputation in this House. I do not believe any man belonging to any group of this House would change his allegiance for any monetary consideration of that kind; we do ourselves a great injustice by making statements of that character in this chamber. Too often we hear from the public platform that men in public life are crooked, and perhaps we cannot blame the public so much if we in this chamber suggest that hon. members of the various groups are not perfectly honourable. I believe the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Brady) is perfectly sincere in his views, and I also think I am quite safe in saying that the gentleman who preceded him as member for that constituency was quite as sincere. Because men hold opposite views is no reason for suggesting that their views are dishonest.
For a few moments now I would like to refer to the remarks of the hon. member for Toronto West Centre (Mr. Hocken), who spoke of a matter which I consider to be of very great importance, dealing with the class of literature coming to Canada from the United States. Again I wish to place myself on record as being in sympathy with a portion of his remarks; I am quite prepared to say with him that I wish to see literature of an immoral character kept out of Canada, whether it comes from the United States or from any other country, but there was one peculiar thing in the remarks of the hon. gentleman. He seemed to mix up immorality in literature with protection, all in the same breath as though he, being a man with a very systematic mind, wished to group together those things which should go together. He held up a magazine which he had described as being obscene and then said in effect, "It

The Budget-Mr. Young (Saskatoon)
comes in free." AVhat was the idea; did he want it to be just a little higher price, a little more expensive? Does he want a higher tariff, so that only the rich can afford to read that obscene literature? In my humble opinion he has taken tlhe wrong ground altogether; he should have said such literature should be prevented from coming into Canada if it is obscene and immoral. I was also very much interested in his argument with respect to the difficulty of printing things in Toronto. He pointed out how difficult if was to do that work there, and took us across to Buffalo to show us how much money could be saved, but his argument at the same time was for protection on those works published in Canada. In developing his argument he said in effect that the price of paper in Toronto was the price of paper in Buffalo plus the duty and plus the freight, and for a few moments he made as fine a speech on free trade as I have ever heard. But he ended in this way, "I do not object to the manufacturer having that protection, but I also ask that the publishing houses should have additional protection." First of all he wants to give protection to the machines and paper and then to the men printing the paper; he wants the whole thing pyramided. And what is he to do with it? We who are the unfortunate consumers have to pay the whole bill; that is one of the difficulties in the argument of the hon. gentleman. If he had confined himself to the question of preventing that class of literature from coming into Canada I think he would have had the sympathy of every member of this House, but when he includes that with higher protection we must disagree.
I would like to go one step further; as a member of this House and a citizen of Canada I am sorry to see so many things on the front pages of our newspapers coming from the United States. There are many little items whidh seem to amuse the people of the United States very much, such as the troubles of Mrs. Aimee Semple McPherson. I assure the House that such things are not of interest to me, but day after day we take up the paper and find pictures of one or two half-wits together with the stories of the crimes they have committed. If the hon. member for Toronto West Centre would pay attention to the prohibition of this class of literature I would be very pleased to give him my support;
For a few moments now I wish to discuss the amendment moved by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote), and first I would like to look at the amendment itself. The words are:
Whilst recognizing the advisability of certain minor changes proposed, this House regrets that
the budget as presented by the honourable Minister of Finance contains no effective provision for the reduction in the high cost of living, in so far as such is due to the protective tariff:
That the budget shows a further departure from the principle of direct and visible taxation based on the ability to pay.
And further that no systematic effort is being made to reduce our national debt, the interest on which absorbs so large a proportion of the revenues of the Dominion.
I particularly wisih to refer for the moment to the last line of the first paragraph, ". . . in so far as such is due to the protective tariff."
I wish to compliment the draftsman of that resolution in the selection of those particular words, which have a very definite purpose and peilhaps some definite meaning, with Which I will deal a little later. Then appear the words, "That the budget shows a further departure from the principle of direct and visible taxation based on the ability to pay." In other words, the suggestion is apparently made that there was regret because of the reduction in the income tax effected by the budget last year, and that now things are getting much worse and we are to have a further reduction. I want to tell the House that I found nothing which gave the common, ordinary people, for whom I stand and whom I represent in this House, greater satisfaction than the fact that they were relieved of that responsibility last year, and until recently I had understood that all hon. members in that particular corner of the House were in agreement with what was then done. I am rather surprised to see how the Robb budget of last year has been handled by certain hon. members in that comer of the House, because last year everyone was apparently satisfied. There are hon. members in this House to-day who were very glad to crawl or creep back to the House tied to the apron strings of that budget; last year they tried to ^hout from the housetops that they were supporters of that budget, and that it was an excellent budget. This year we have another such budget, but this year we have the amendment I have already read.
I would call your attention now to an amendment brought up in this House last year by the present Prime Minister, which was as follows:
That the Speaker do not now leave the chair but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this House the fiscal policy of the government, as enunciated by the present Prime Minister when leader of His Majesty's opposition, would prove detrimental to the country's continued prosperity and prejudicial to national unity.

Upon the hearing before Your Excellency in Council it appeared that the re-establishment of the rates provided for in the Crowsnest pass agreement upon the limited list of commodities and between the points specified therein had brought about considerable variations in the rates applicable thereto prior to the 7th July, 1924, and it was urged on behalf of a large section of the Dominion, and in particular by counsel for the cities of Edmonton, Alberta, and Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, and the maritime provinces, as well as representatives of responsible trade organizations in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec that the establishment of these rates would disrupt the rate structure built up under the control of the board since its creation, with consequent serious injury to trade relationships throughout the Dominion.
It was also urged that sources of supply had changed since the agreement was made and that certain commodities which were formerly shipped in large quantities from eastern Canada to the prairie provinces are now largely supplied either by local industries or from British Columbia, which latter province, it was alleged, would be cut off from a large part of its natural market by the permanent restoration of the Crowsnest rates.
It was further urged that the continuance of the Crowsnest rates (so-called) would compel the Canadian National Railways to make similar reductions from all competitive points, and thus involve a serious loss in revenue to them which would have to be made up from other government sources and further postpone the time when it would be possible to make any general rate readjustment or to solve satisfactorily the problem of the National Railways.
The committee observe that the agreement in question was made at a time when the Canadian Pacific Railway Company was the only company having a through line of railway extending through the prairie provinces and British Columbia, and before the creation of the board for the control of railway rates

under the provisions of the Railway Act of 1903 and subsequent acts; and further, that the underlying purpose of the rate control inaugurated by the Railway Act of 1903 was to do away as far as possible with all unjust discriminations and undue preferences, and to secure a fair and reasonable rate structure, which, under substantially similar circumstances and conditions would be equal in its application to all persons and localities.
The committee are of the opinion that the policy of equalization of freight rates should be recognized to the fullest possible extent as being the only means of dealing equitably with all parts of Canada, and as being the method best calculated to facilitate the interchange of commodities between the various portions of the Dominion, as well as the encouragement of industry and agriculture and the development of export trade.
The committee are further of the opinion that to give effect to this policy, and considering the submissions made by counsel and important trade organizations representing different provinces and localities in the Dominion as to the disadvantages that would be suffered by such provinces and localities by any partial or incomplete consideration of the freight rate structure, a thorough and complete investigation of the whole subject of railway freight rates in the Dominion should be carried out by the Board of Railway Commissioners, the body constituted by parliament with full powers under statute to fix and control railway rates.
The committee are further of the opinion that as the production and export of grain and flour forms one of the chief assets of the Dominion, and in order to encourage the further development of the great grain growing provinces of the west, on which development the future of Canada in large measure depends, it is desirable that the maximum cost of the transportation of these products should be determined and known, and therefore are of opinion that the maximum established for rates on grain and flour, as at present in force under the Crowsnest pass agreement, should not be exceeded.
The committee are further of the opinion that, before such investigation is undertaken it is essential to ensure that the provisions of the Railway Act in reference to tariffs and tolls, and the jurisdiction of the board thereunder. be unfettered by any limitations other than the provisions as to grain and flour hereinbefore mentioned.

Unless this country can afford us men of the right stamp, men of independence of character, of firmness, and of fairness, men who have experience in business, experience in railway operations, experience in law, unless the country can afford us these conditions, then, we cannot look with any reasonable hope to find that the operation of the commission will be successful.
Then again at page 2439:
We think it is desirable; indeed we think it imperative on us to prevent the possibility of persons who feel they may have grievances against railways not being able to have their cases determined within a reasonable time. We have therefore asked parliament to say that the decision of this tribunal shall be final, subject only to revision by the privy council, and that there shall be an appeal to no other tribunal.

The Budget-Mr. Young (Saskatoon)
In the same volume of Hansard, at page 2453, Mr. T. O. Davis, formerly representative of Prince Albert, later Senator Davis, now deceased, spoke as follows:
As I have stated before in this House, it is a well known fact that the trade and business of this country have grown at such a rate that it is impossible for the railway committee of the privy council to handle the business it should handle in connection with matters of this kind that come before it. As a matter of fact we know, from our own experience in the west this year,-
That was twenty-five years ago:
-that the people there have lost a great amount of money from the fact that we have had no body of this kind to regulate the railways of the country.
We want a body appointed that will see that there is no discrimination in rates.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have given these two quotations with the object of showing what was in the minds of those responsible for the passing of this legislation. And who was more capable of passing an opinion on a matter of this kind than the late Hon. A. G. Blair? He recognized that there must not be delay, that when a matter of this kind comes up before some body that body must be a capable one, it must be trained' in the law, it must be trained in business. But the thing on which the statesmen of that time were unanimous was that there must be no delay in giving out decisions. What have wre got in this particular case? Here we have a board and it is now investigating grain rates. I want to differentiate this afternoon very clearly between the general freight rates inquiry and the statute making the Crowsnest agreement rates apply over a wider territory. The order in council passed *on the 5th of June directed that there should be a general freight rate inquiry and to that, of course, I take no exception. But on 27th June, 1925- and if you notice it is now over twenty months since that was done-the parliament of Canada by statute said that the rates under the law of 1897, the Crowsnest pass agreement, should apply to all the other sections of Canada, and to-day, after a lapse of twenty months, those rates do not apply. It is true that several hearings have taken place. The hearing of the Bell Telephone Company's application for an increase in rates has taken place. That hearing was started on January 26th, 1926, and we already have the decision by the Board of Railway Commissioners with respect to telephone rates in this part of Canada. What is the difference between the two? The statutory provision in connection with the Crowsnest pass agreement removes a burden from the mass of primary producers in western Canada. The application cf the Bell Telephone Company deals with an increase in telephone rates of subscribers in eastern Canada. The Bell Telephone Company application has been heard and decided and the company has been granted permission to increase its rates. The statutory provision based on the Crowsnest pass agreement has not been carried out, and1 I want to say that when this parliament passes a statute no three members of the Board of Railway Commissioners or any other body has any right to set that statute at nought. The board before whom this hearing took place consists of six members, five of whom come from eastern Canada and one from the west. They divided on a fifty-fifty basis, and because of that the will of parliament is set at nought. Everyone knows that there is at present a discriminatory rate on grain in the northern part of Saskatchewan, the northern part of Alberta, the northern part of Manitoba. But we in Saskatchewan are affected to a greater degree than the other provinces because we ship more grain. It means the application of an additional two cents per hundred pounds on grain moving eastward to all that northern country. This represents to the primary producers, the farmers of that section of country, a loss of between one and two million dollars a year. Why are they suffering this loss? Because the Board of Railway Commissioners have r.ot seen fit, apparently do not wish to do so even at this late date, to permit a statute of parliament to apply to these railway rates. But the Bell Telephone Company have been given permission to increase their telephone rates although there is no specific statute of parliament behind them. If we were now, Mr. Speaker, in the throes of a campaign to raise a victory loan and the farmers of northern Saskatchewan, of northern Alberta and of northern Manitoba were being asked to subscribe to the loan and took, we will say, 82,000,000 of victory bonds, their action would be regarded as most patriotic and the investment would be looked upon as an excellent one. If they subscribed to that-and the farmers in my part of the country subscribed for and took. $2,000,000 of those debentures which were splendid, paying debentures-they would then be regarded as most patriotic people for taking an excellent investment. To-day, what do we see? We have the same farmers in that same portion of the country from whom is being taken annually unjustly and unfairly, the sum of about $2,000,000, just because the Board of Railway Commissioners

The Budget-Mr. Young (Saskatoon)
will not see to it that the railways put into operation the statutory rates as passed by the parliament of Canada.
Perhaps if I speak with some heat I may be pardoned. I am always very happy when I am speaking for the primary producers of this country, and all they ask is that they be given what the parliament of Canada said they should get. I am not arguing that the rates should be higher or lower. That is not the question at all. That question has been settled. We have been waiting for twenty months for these rates to be put into operation and for all we know we may have to wait for twenty months more. We have had two crops move under the discriminatory rates. Is that fair?
I come now to another matter and I want to quote just one more section from the Railway Act. Section 44 states:
The governor in council may, at any time, in his discretion, either upon petition of any party, person or company interested, or of his own motion and without any petition or application therefor, vary, change, or rescind any order, decision, rule or regulation of the board, whether such order or decision be made inter partes or otherwise, and whether such regulation be general or limited in its scope and application; and any order which the governor in council may make with respect thereto shall be binding on the board and all parties.
Further, section 45 states:
The governor in council may at any time refer to the board for a report, or other action, any question, matter or thing arising, or required to be done, under this act, or the special act, and the board shall without delay comply therewith.
I understand that an appeal from the Board of Railway Commissioners has been made to the government that the Crowsnest pass agreement as extended shall be made to apply.
I am now going to appeal to the Minister of Finance, to every other minister in the House at this moment, and, indeed, to all ministers of t'he crown that due consideration be given to the appeal made by counsel on behalf of the western provinces. I do not, as a general rule, approve appeals from the board to the government on matters of fact. If we get into a situation of that kind, it will be unfortunate. I do not blame the government for refusing appeals of that character. But here we have an appeal in which all that is being asked is that a statute of the parliament of Canada be lived up to, be adhered to.
I am going to urge again that this government give consideration to the appeal made, and that it direct that the Board of Railway Commissioners render judgment accordingly and see that all discriminations are removed.

What is the situation? We have before the Board of Railway Commissioners all the tariffs filed. We have gone to the limit. We have an array of counsel in the city of Ottawa before the board and all they are doing is bringing up all kinds of technicalities. This board should be primarily a business organization with some law in it. On the contrary it is, as at present constituted, a legal institution with practically no business in it. We want to have this condition of affairs reversed. I have always had and I hope I shall always have the greatest respect for the legal profession, but at the same time we have too many technicalities creeping into this board, which has too many lawyers on it. This board was created for the purpose, not of bringing in all kinds of technicalities, but of hastening decisions.
What is required to be done with regard to the statutory rates is simply this. Every schedule of the railways was available to the Board of Railway Commissioners and the statute said:	There shall be no excuse for
discrimination. Surely it was not necessary with those schedules before them to have all the counsel from western Canada come to Ottawa and have the board examine them. Some good might have been accomplished by their sitting down without any counsel and finding out whether discrimination existed. They cannot say that the trouble is that they did not have counsel, because, heaven knows! we sent enough counsel down. The counsel are here, but what are we getting?
I have taken a long time to place these facts on the record, but I believe they should be on record and every one should know what has taken place, namely, nothing but unwarranted delay. Before I sit down I again ask the government to request, to demand, from the Board of Railway Commissioners that judgment be issued immediately, or we may have to wait so long that another crop will have to be moved under these disermina-tory rates. If we cannot get speedy enough action from the present Board of Railway Commissioners, we must have a new board that will act with promptness.
I am going to make two or three suggestions and the first one is this. The board tell us very frankly that if they divide fifty-fifty, they cannot come to a decision. We must see to it that they cannot divide fifty-fifty, and we must therefore have an odd number on the board. In the second place-and I want to insist upon this as far as I have any power to insist upon anything-I want to see one-half of the board come from western Canada. To-day we have on the board six men, five

The Budget-Mr. Chaplin
of whom come from tfhe east and one from the west, and at this very moment from Fort William and Port Arthur west there are more miles of railway than there are in eastern Canada. Third, I want on the board rather than men of legal minds, men of business capacity who will deal with matters expeditiously, men who will not deliberately set aside an act of parliament.
Unless we get those things, the unrest which we have in western Canada in regard to this matter will not subside, but will increase. We cannot afford to allow a thing of this kind to delay any longer, and I am going to plead once more with the government to see to it that at the earliest passible date the defects that now exist in the Board of Railway Commissioners are removed.
In closing let me say that I am a very staunch admirer of the institution of the Board of Railway Commissioners. I do not know of anything which can replace it; but I have observed, and I am not alone in observing, that during the last several years the. board has been getting farther and farther away from being a board and closer and closer to being a court, the very situation it was created to obviate. I remember hearing one of the chief commissioners some time ago, when a poor unfortunate widow came before the board and a lawyer was sent up from one of the big corporations, saying to him: Stand aside; I want to hear what the poor woman has to say. We want more of that spirit on the board, and if we have it, the primary producers will not have to have their representatives in this House taking up the whole afternoon in laying their case before the House, because they will receive prompt justice. Let me again urge the government to take prompt and effective action.

The hon. member who has just resumed his seat (Mr. Young, Saskatoon) took up the early part of his speech in reading several lectures to different members of the House, particularly the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote), because Of the fact that he put on the order paper a resolution which the government finds somewhat embarrassing. He forgets that at the last session of parliament, almost during the dying hours of the session, one of the very things that was done was to introduce a similar resolution, and just for a moment I intend to refer to it. On the 30th of June, after the Mackenzie King government had been defeated, a resolution was brought in for the purpose of disturbing my friends to my left who had helped to defeat that government. Here is the resolution:
That the Speaker do not now leave the chair, but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this House the fiscal policy of the government as enunciated by the present Prime Minister when leader of His Majesty's opposition would prove detrimental to the country's continued prosperity and prejudicial to the national unity.
That was the resolution that was brougnt in, and moreover the hon. member who has just spoken, and who talks of political resolutions, voted for that resolution, as is shown by the division list in Hansard. So he deprecates in others the very thing he did himself only a short time ago.
Did the hon. member ask me a question? I would like to say, Mr. Speaker-

Mr. Speaker, I object. The hon. gentleman asked a question, and then he starts out to make a statement. He has taken up two hours of the time of this House, and surely he can keep quiet now for a minute and take a little of the medicine I am going to give him.
I thought you asked me a question.

I never asked you a question at all. It was you who started to ask a question, and then went on to make a statement.
The hon. member had something further to say about the tariff board. Oh, he says, we will give them dots of time; we must be fair and reasonable. Now I make this Statement: My hon. friend1, and many other hon. members for years have been telling the people of the northwest what they could do in fifteen minutes in respect to the tariff; it would not take more ithan that length of time to decide the whole thing. Give the board a fair and reasonable time? The leader of my hon. friend's party, in a pronouncement made at the Liberal convention in 1919, a good many years ago, told us definitely what his party were going to do. But they are still there; they never did it.
My hon. friend does not always get his own way with respect to the railway board, and he took up a lot of the time of the House this afternoon in reading at length from the records, and he threatens that if this and that is not done there is going to be trouble with the northwest. "We are going to get the Same number on that board from the west as from the east," he says, "because of the mileage in our part of the country." Did you ever

hear a more preposterous proposition? "We are going to 'have half the membership of the board." Is that fair and reasonable? I do not mind if they never make a report. They can postpone making their recommendations for ever, so far as I am concerned. One of the things I find fault with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) about is that he had this board appointed which looks like an effort to avoid making a pronouncement on tariff matters by the government, and more than that, after the board is appointed the budget is brought down early so that the government will not have a dhance of doing anything about the tariff this year anyway.
Before I say what I have to say on the budget, I want to refer to an address made here a few dayis ago by the kon. member for Macleod (Mr. Ooote), and to some statements that he made. I regret very much that the hon. member is not in bis seat to-day; I would much prefer that he were here. A few days ago he placed on Hansard several statements, and right here, Mr. Speaker, let me say that I notice a growing disposition on the part of members to have statements and papers handed to the reporter so that they can be put upon Hansard, contrary to the rules and usage of the House. I have expected the ministers to stop that practice. It is not my place to do it, but I call attention to the matter, and point out that statements have been repeatedly put on Hansard without being read, and some of them are not correct. The one that I am going to refer to is an instance of that.
I looked up Hansard the day after the hon. member for Macleod spoke, and found the statement that he had placed on Hansard without reading it. The statement is not correct. It is very incorrect and irregular;
I might use a very much stronger word, Mr. Speaker, but knowing the gentleman as I do, knowing that he has always been fair, I attribute this inaccuracy to his want of knowledge of the subject. I will just quote from page 501 of Hansard what he had to say:
I have a table here, compiled from the statistics of the Department of Trade and Commerce for the year 1925, and which I will place on Hansard, if I have the permission of the House, showing that our agricultural, vegetable and animal products amount to 56 per cent of our total exports. The table is as follows-
Then the table follows. I had naturally expected, Mr. Speaker, that when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) 
followed the hon. member for Macleod, he would correct those figures, but of course the minister was under the disadvantage of not knowing what they were. I will take the figures in the statement one by one, giving only the round numbers.
It shows that our exports in 1925 of agricultural and vegetable products amounted to $443,000,000. Now on examining the returns I find that the items bulked under the heading of animal and vegetable products total $443,000,000, but the hon. member never looked to see what those items consisted ot I am just going to show from another page, for the information of the House, just exactly what those items consisted of that make up this $443,000,000, and which with the animal products comprise, according to the hon. member for Macleod, 56 per cent of our exports.

Can the hon. gentleman show where the member for Macleod refers to that as a product of the farm?
Mr. Speaker, the whole basis of his argument was that fifty-six per cent of the total exports of Canada came from the farm. What else could this mean?

[Mr. Chaplin.l
wonderful results that have ensued. I can assure the House that he is hardly recognizable as the same man.

If you had seen him at

I do not know anything

This is a question of privilege. I was asked to come to Ottawa by the Minister of Finance and other ministers of the govemmemt for the purpose of assisting them in any way possible in the matter of automobiles.

In closing I want to say just a word or two regarding the result of same of the treaties that this government has put its hand to. We have discussed the treaty with France which we have had on the statute books for a number of years, and I want to direct attention to some of the latest consequences of that agreement. Of the nine months of the present year ending December 31 we bought from France $17,346,000 worth of goods, whereas during the same period we sold them around $7,000,000 worth. During the full fiscal year 1925 we bought from them $18,500,000 and sold them $10,500,000. When this treaty was entered into, imports and1 exports were practically on a level; to-day our imports from France have increased except for a few items, while a long list of goods we formerly sold them has vanished from our export returns. To-day we sell them wheat and sugar, wood pulp, salmon, lobsters and a few ores such as lead and cobalt, as well as asbestos, coal and tar. In addition to these we sell them two items of manufactured goods, rubber tires and, to some extent, agricultural implements. But goods that we formerly supplied to France, goods that were embodied in (the treaty, enumerated by the hundreds, we no longer sell to that country. We are selling to France only the purest raw material while we are buying from them an increased amount of goods, chiefly luxuries, on which we deliberately reduced the duties in order to facilitate the importation of them into Canada. This reduction in duty is now costing the treasury of the country between three and four million dollars, counting in the goods from other countries that came in to take advantage of the French treaty. That is what the treaty with France has cost us. If it is a matter of sentiment and not of business, by all means let us trade with France on that basis; but if we have an eye to business, then I contend that the treaty is bad. I so described it at the time the treaty was drawn up. I said before it came into effect that it would be harmful and it has turned out that way without question. The then 
Minister of Marine, now Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), who made the treaty, told us at the time wonderful stories about the butter and other commodities we would sell to France. But there has not been a pound of butter sold. At any rate, we have not sold enough of that article to make a smell in a pan. Our trade in cheese is gone and the milk we used to sell to France in canned form we are no longer selling.

From appearances the debate on the budget is drawing to a close, or at any rate is on the last lap. The government, to the best of its ability, has defended its inaction and its reaction, and the party to my right has criticised the budget in the usual manner and put forward its ideas. The group with which I am associated has done likewise. All that I would wish to say on the budget has therefore been already said by my colleagues in this section of the chamber, and I regard the repetition of arguments about as tiresome when, it comes from a number of persons as when it comes from an individual. For that reason it is essential for me to make some explanation as to why I venture to speak at all at this time. My object in rising is mainly to reply to an attack which was made by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) on the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) in respect of the speech he delivered the other evening. Not only did the minister attack the hon. member in a more or less personal way, but he also attacked the entire farmers' movement, and particularly the group to which I belong. That speech was made on Thursday night last, and it was of such a character that it did not do justice to the argument of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland); it did not add much credit to the minister who made the attack nor did it reflect much credit on the government in the defence of which he spoke. I think the attack was regrettable, not only because we expected something better from the minister but also because the minister was very well qualified, if he had so chosen, to defend the government and answer the arguments of the hon. member on a much higher plane than he selected. I am bound to concede at the outset of my remarks that in natural gifts as well as in long experience in public life the Minister of Railways is one of the outstanding men in Canadian public life to-day. He was elevated from that obscurity with which I think most immigrants find themselves surrounded to the position of premier of his province, and after serving with considerable distinction in that honoured position he was called to take charge of that most important department which he now directs. These facts emphasize the ability of the hon. gentleman and also mark the fact that his fellow citizens have recognized that ability. With his great gifts and his opportunities to gain knowledge,
together with his long experience in public life, we expected a great deal from him when he rose in his seat to explain the budget and to give the reasons for the inaction on the part of the government in implementing their program of promises to the Canadian people. His failure to so much as refer to some of the questions of public importance, after his attention -was drawn to them by the hon. member for Bow River, is to be regretted, but the nature and spirit of his reply is even more to be regretted. I was personally very much astonished at the attitude the minister took, the more so because of the exalted opinion of the minister held by the public generally.

I want to follow the main points of the argument made by the hon. member for Bow River in order to show that the reply given was not satisfactory, that the points the minister did attempt to reply to were unsatisfactorily answered, and that his eloquent silence on other points is something worthy of note. The hon. member for Bow River opened his remarks by charging that the present budget was a rich man's budget, and he also referred to the reduction in income tax as the reduction feature of the budget. He went on to argue that since the income tax is paid only by those who have sufficient income to come within the scope of the act, it goes without saying that the reduction in the income tax will favour those who are most wealthy, and indeed it does not affect the poorer classes of the community at all. That was the basis of his charge, that it was a rich man's budget. But what did the minister reply to that? It is an extremely interesting reply; it is worthy of contemplation and profound study. His first argument was that it is very difficult to apply the income tax, so difficult to apply indeed that it is an unsurmountable problem. He quoted, I think, from some individual farmer whom he did not mention and that individual farmer went on to say that "we go to forty dollars' worth of time and trouble to find out that we owe the government $10." Now let me refer the minister to the propaganda of the Liberal party. What does that propaganda say about the tariff tax? Does the hon. minister mean to say that the tariff tax is more easily imposed, more easily and more cheaply collected

than the income tax? I think I have read somewhere in Liberal propaganda that it takes $3 to collect $1 of revenue from the tariff tax.

Now I appreciate this conviction which the minister had, but I would have appreciated it very much more if he had acquainted us with the process of reasoning by which he arrived at it. He says that under the present tax a farmer spends $40 worth of time in discovering that he owes the government $10. The minister now proposes to reduce the tax by ten per cent which will mean that the farmer will spend $40 and find out that he owes the government $1. And then the hon. gentleman tells us that this reduction was made in the interests of the farmers. The minister did not wipe the thing out so that the farmers would not come under its operation. They have got to make a report to the government officials to discover whether they owe anything under this ten per cent reduction or not, just as they did before. Therefore the reason the minister acted in the interests of the farmer is so obscure, to say the least, that I am unable to detect the hon. gentleman's reasoning. I think he could have done better by increasing the amount of exemption and then increasing the amount of taxation upon the amount fixed. In that way peirhaps he would have helped the farmers to better advantage.
Now if the finances of the Dominion warrant tax reduction, a reduction should have been made first of that taxation which falls more heavily upon the mass of the people, that tax which is a decided burden to the agricultural population at the present time- that of the tariff. More especially should this have been done when to accomplish such
reduction is one of the professed policies of the Liberal party. The tariff question is the hobby-horse of Canadian politics. I have never ridden that hobby; I refuse to straddle that antiquated mechanism. But in the interests of political honesty we are bound to insist that the present administration either implement the promises that they have made to the Canadian people from time to time, and justify their adherence to a policy of tariff reduction, or else frankly admit that it cannot be done or that they will not do it. The Liberal party surely will not deny that it has committed itself, in the eloquent words of the Prime Minister, to "a downward revision policy." I think that that right hon. gentleman also drafted the chart which led down gradually from the high tariff of the Conservative party to the free trade policy which is peculiar to the Liberals. That chart they started to follow, but through some strange, unexplained reason, they have suddenly abandoned it. It is true that under pressure! of the Progressive group in the last parliament they attempted an experiment by reducing the tariff taxes on automobiles, and indeed it was that reduction of automobile taxation that enabled the present party on the right of the Speaker to come into power. During the last election whenever a Conservative candidate mentioned anything about Customs scandal, the Liberal candidate jumped into one of these automobiles and scurried for his life, and the Liberals thereby got into power. I am not, however, overlooking the charge of the Conservative party that the tax reduction on automobiles reduced the revenue of the country, which reduction had to be made up by taxing everybody else that much more; nor am I forgetting the charge that the automobile industry obtained certain concessions which offset the tariff reductions. That is another part of the question which I am not addressing myself to now.
I am content for the present to take the words of the Minister of Finance on this question. He very clearly pointed out that the direct effect of that reduction was that the government collected more revenue and that the automobile industry flourished. That is what the Liberals always contended would happen when they reduced taxes. The minister was, I imagine, very glad ,to be able to report that what they had anticipated was so in fact. They gained more revenue by reducing the tax and the automobile industry flourished. Does the Minister of Finance know that there are in Canada a number of industries that would like to get some of that prosperity? Does he not know

also that the finances of this country could stand a little more of that revenue coming in so handily and that the people of Canada would be pleased to get at a lower price the goods which these industries are manufacturing? That is the question that I want the government to answer, the question which the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) ran away from when it was placed before him by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland)? I want any member of the government to answer that question now or to answer it some time before this debate closes.
If they were telling the truth about the automobile business-and I am not for one moment doubting their word-that by the reduction in the tariff on automobiles more automobiles were sold, the business flourished and the taxes collected amounted to more than previously, what is the excuse which the government offers for not repeating that in regard to other industries? That is a reasonable question. It grows out of the professed policy of the government itself; it actually flows out of the philosophy of the Liberal party, and we want to know why they have retarded this prosperity by their inaction. That question still remains to be answered, and I hope the Minister of Railways, when he speaks from now on regarding any question . relating to the tariff, will do what he did not do the other day, and answer it to the satisfaction of the House. Now I ask-that the government either follow the chart towards the lower tariff goal or frankly state that such a policy cannot be followed.
Some hon. members speaking in this debate said that the present budget was a Conservative budget. I disagree with that. I think this is a typically Liberal budget. It has been defended by a typical Liberal and the policy which the minister announced is also typically Liberal. The budget is typically Liberal becauses it does not do one thing that can be defended from the point of view of Liberal philosophy. If this had been a Conservative budget brought in by Conservatives,
I will give them this credit at least to say that they would have defended it on the ground that the industries of Canada required such protection, and rightly or wrongly, very probably wrongly, they would have defended that to the last ditch. But when we ask a Liberal government to defend this budget, what do they say? The last speaker on the Liberal side (Mr. Young, Saskatoon) said that the Minister of Finance was too tired to lower the tariff. The Minister of Railways said that they did not have time to lower the tariff. They had time to leave it alone, did they not? These are petty excuses, un-

worthy of the history of Liberalism, unworthy of great Liberals, and I think if hon. gentlemen opposite had an eye to the future, they would thank us for endeavouring to press them to be true to their own philosophy. Those are, I say, unworthy subterfuges, unworthy of the hon. gentlemen advancing them.
But a more characteristic excuse even than these' was advanced by the Minister of Railways. In reply to the hon. member for Bow River, he said that the second reason why the tariff had not been reduced in this budget was that they did not have all the facts. He charged the hon. member for Bow River with being the type of man who wants the tariff reduced whether he has the facts or not, and he charged this whole group with being of a similar character. We do not mind the minister's raillery, if I may use his own word; but I ask the minister and the government this question If that is the reason why they have not altered the tariff, would it not have been far better if the Liberal party had taken that attitude fifty years ago? It is a fine time now to tell us that they cannot alter the tariff because they have not the facts. Would it not have been better if they had secured the facts before they formulated a policy?
If we look at the literature which their publicists issued in the lasit election, did they tell the people of Canada: Oh, after we have all the facts we shall see what we can do with this tariff business? Did their candidates say to the people of the west: Oh, after we have all the facts, we will sit down, scratch our heads for a while and see if we can take a little bit off here and add a little bit on there? They did not do that. They went out on a low tariff policy. They did not say: Our tariff policy will depend on the facts and we have not gathered them yet. I am not objecting to the facts being secured; I think it would be a splendid thing to get the facts, but I am simply pointing out to the minister that if he is going to get stuck on facts now, it would have been better if he had got stuck on them a long time ago because far less misrepresentation would then have followed the course of the Liberal party.
Let me now turn to the master apologia of the minister. With that characteristic flourish of his he said: What would have happened if we had actually taken action on flake calcium chloride, nail kegs, Epsom salts, foxes and canaries? He said: Hon. members of this assembly, what would have happened if we had taken action on those things? Well, what would have happened? What is going to happen now that the hon. gentleman did

not take action on these foxes and canaries? The foxes have holes and the canaries have nests, but the farmers of. Canada are unable to pay anything on income tax because their incomes are not big enough. Therefore I think it would have been wise if the minister had not made that remark, which is rather unbecoming and which would seem to indicate that either he took the subject less seriously than a man in his position should, or perhaps' we may have overestimated his ability. We are left to guess .at the policy now to be followed by the Liberal party, and my guess is as good as anybody else's. I want to make three guesses as to what is going to happen to this Liberal policy henceforth, and I am going to guess so comprehensively that I do not think I can be wrong.
My first guess is that this government, when it came to make up its budget for 1927, discovered that the tariff as left by the Conservative government some years ago was t.he best kind of tariff for the people of Canada. They discovered that they could not disturb that tariff without disturbing the industries of Canada, and so in the best interests of industry, and in the best interests of the people, they refrained from touching the tariff at all. But having discovered that, they would not come to parliament and so state, because if they had done so they would have openly acknowledged the virtue of the Conservative policy, and would have given hostages to their enemy with a vengeance. That is my first guess. I do not know whether it is right or not, and so I am going to cover the field of guessing as to what the government's policy is.
My next guess is that the government, when it started to make up its budget for this year, was convinced that the policy of the Liberal party, 'that of a revision downwards of the tariff from time to time, was the best policy, and that they sincerely desired to put it into effect; but when they actually came to make up the budget and to implement their policy foy tariff reduction they found they could not do it for one of two reasons; one being that they had so many high tariff men in their ranks that they did not dare to lower the tariff, or else this is my second guess -there was so much influence outside the party as to prevent the government taking the action they had promised to take. If that foe right, then I argue that the government of the day should have risked its policy on a vote in parliament, should have gone out of power honourably, if need be, and come back with renewed strength to carry out its policy, rather
than sit quietly and do nothing but make apologies to the people of Canada for having failed.
I do not know whether the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) or the hon. member for Quebec-Montmoreney (Mr. Lavigueur) is speaking for the government in this matter, but I rather suspect that the latter gentleman was giving the true policy of the Liberal party when he spoke, and I think his opening remarks are very significant. I wish to quote them in support of one of my guesses. The hon. gentleman says:
I consider it an honour to follow the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail), the only .lady in the House of Commons, although I do not share her views generally, and particularly so far as the tariff is concerned. I am pleased to see that the budget this year contains no items of reduction.
I think you will agree with me that my guess number two is a good one, but if that is so, the Liberal .party cannot expect to go on forever in that position. There will come a time when they will have to make a break, and they might as well make it now. If the Liberal party has so many high tariff men in its ranks, let them go to the high .tariff party, and let the Liberal party, if it is going .to stand for anything, come out and stand for it.
There is another possible explanation, although the Minister of Railways denied this emphatically in answer .to a question put by the hon. member for Bow River. This guess is that the government intends henceforth to leave tariff adjustments to the advice of the Tariff Advisory Board, and to abandon the policy of downward revisions of the tariff, because if they leave it to the advice of the tariff board there might be an upward revision; we do not know what kind of revision the board will recommend. Personally-I am speaking purely for myself, and not for my group at all in this matter -I think that the latter course would be preferable to the one that is now being followed. I do not think that there can foe any less hope of a tariff board finding a solution of the tariff question than we can have in either of the old parties finding it. May I take the opportunity here, Mr. Speaker, to point out what appears to me to be a very grave danger indeed to Canada, arising from the historic conflict between the Conservatives and the Liberals over the tariff? We have developed undoubtedly what is known to-day as a west and an east. That is not a geographical division; it is a division of sentiment; it is a division of the people more distinct than could be effected by geography. That division has largely come about through the propaganda of these two parties which I address to-night in this House. Canada, I say, is divided between east and west. The farmers and manufacturers are at loggerheads. We have a struggle between what has been called by some hon. member of this House the robbed and the robbers. I think the House will agree with me that it will take more than a few after-dinner speeches, inspired by choice viands and a glass of champagne, to offset sixty years of the type of propaganda to which I have referred. Ever since the days of Sir John A. Macdonald up to the present time the propaganda of the Liberal party has been such as to lead the agricultural population in Canada to believe that our manufacturers are just so many profiteers who use the tariff as an easy way to make money. of Canada outside of parliament and to the organized manufacturers of Canada outside of parliament that they take this matter in their own hands and settle it as it should be settled. If that can be done in international affairs,

To begin with, let me say that in Cleveland a few months ago, last fall I think it was, the United States offered prizes in an endeavour to find out the champion state and the champion grower of two varieties of vegetables, celery and cauliflower. They threw that competition open to Canada, and Canadian growers came home with both championships. It shows that we have efficient producers in this country. But what I particularly wish to draw attention to is that in the United States the gardeners and vegetable growers have three markets, two high priced and one low priced. The gardeners and vegetable growers of Canada have only one market, and that low priced. What are these markets? The United States growers have first the early market in their own country, which is the high priced market. Then they get our early and high priced market. They have also of course the later market in the United States, which is the low priced market. We permit this dumping of American produce, for it is nothing else. As time elapsed a crop of tomatoes in a more northerly district of the United States began to ripen. This crop was not a failure. A few warm days and a huge surplus of southern tomatoes existed. Brokers in a frantic effort to save domestic markets re-shipped and reshipped; trainloads of tomatoes began to crowd closer to the border. Because there is an exportable surplus of wheat; and furthermore the farmers are not organized.

So that,
according to my hon. friend, the argument applies only where there is not an exportable surplus. I shall have to leave the hon. gentleman to work that out. If that argument means anything it means that the farmers get over $10,000,000 a year extra on wheat because of that 12 cent duty. Take butter: we produce about 300,000,000 pounds of butter a year and levy a duty of 4 cents. We had an exportable surplus last year of about 24,500,000 pounds. According to the argument of Mr. Mackenzie, the 4 cents duty is paid by the people on all butter that is made in Canada as well as on all that is imported.
Some hon. MEMBERS. No.

According
to my hon. friends the argument does not apply to eggs or anything that the farmer

produces; it has reference only to things that are manufactured. Very well. I have stated my position and I leave it to my hon. friend to wrestle with the question at his leisure.
Even Adam Smith has acknowledged that a protective tariff may result in cheapening production. A common free trade fallacy is that the duty raises the cost irrespective of the volume of production not affected by the duty. That is the free trader's commonest fallacy. Price is determined by supply and demand and the duty can affect it only so far as the untaxed supply does not meet the demand. There are two cardinal errors free traders fall into: one is that the burden of the import duty must fall entirely on the consumer, and the other is that the tariff must increase the cost of the article taxed. Both these assumptions are fallacious; they are wrong, as time and history have demonstrated hundreds of times.
There are two distinct classes of import duties. There are the free trade duties imposed on such things as we do not and cannot produce in this country, such, for example, as tea and coffee. In such cases the whole amount of the duty is paid by the consumer. There is nothing to come in competition with such commodities, because they are not produced within, our borders. There is another kind of duty also-protective duties levied on articles which are or can be produced in the country. Here the primary object is to increase home production and give employment. Here only a portion, is subject to duty while a greater or lesser portion is free. Here there is active competition between the dutiable and the duty free portions, and obviously the importer cannot pass on the whole duty to the consumer. The extent to which he can do so depends on two things: the extent to which he will be able to pass the tax on depends, first, on the amount of competition between the home producers of the article, and, secondly, the amount of competition between the dutiable and the duty free supplies.
Mr. Bonar Law, discussing this point, used these words:
The consumer pays the duty they say and I suppose most of them believe that this is an axiom of political economy. It is an axiom only of the platform; it is not an axiom of the study. No economist living or dead ever made such a statement. The extent to which the import duty will be paid by the consumer depends entirely on circumstances, and the chief circumstance on which it depends is the amount of the competition between the duty paying and the duty free supply.
I have heard (the question asked, if the duty does not raise the price what is the use of it to the producer? I want to give the

words of a political economist in answer to that question, because they enunciate the principle on which the Conservative party stands. The purpose of protection is not to raise prices but to defend and develop the purchasing power of the nation, one of the most important duties of government, and thereby maintain and improve employment, wages, and the standards of living of those dependent directly or indirectly on the nation's producing industries, which means, in effect, the entire population of the country. John Stuart Mill has said:
The only mode in which a country can save itself from being a loser by the revenue duties imposed by other countries on its commodities is to impose corresponding duties on theirs.
Throw away that weapon and what have you left to protect yourself with? Lord Balfour on December 5, 1923, said:
I have always been in favour of using o'" power of putting on taxation on foreign goods where it seemed desirable for the purpose _ of enabling us to negotiate arrangements with foreign countries upon basis favourable to our own manufacturers.
There is just one other matter to which I want to refer, and I do so because there was a reference made to it in the speech of the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McMillan) the other day. The hon. member gave a number of interesting figures to prove his contention that the farmers of Canada were more prosperous than the farmers of the United States. He quoted figures in regard to the decrease in the number of farms, and s0 on-all this with the purpose of showing that the farmers here were better off than those across the line. With that statement I have no wish to disagree, but I should like that hon. gentleman to carry his study a little further. I can assure any hon. member who wishes to spend a few interesting days considering this subject that he will find it very enlightening indeed to examine, as I have done, the census statistics of the United States for the year 1910 as compared with the year 1920. If he does so, he will find that in 1920 there were 191,073 fewer farms and 3,726,527 less improved acreage in twenty-four of the forty-eight states of the union. And in every one of these states there was an increase in the mortgage indebtedness in relation to 'land value. There are still twenty-four other states to be accounted for. Examining the figures, I found that these states that show an increase in the number of farms in 1920 as compared with 1910, and an increase in the improved farm acreage, together with a decrease in the mortgage indebtedness in

The Budget-Mr. Edwards (Frontenac)
relation to land values, are the southern states. What do we learn from that fact? We can get a lesson from it. The twenty-four states that show a decrease in the number of farms and improved farm acreage, together with an increase in the mortgage indebtedness, are northern states which, with one or two exceptions, have the same sort of climate as we have in Ontario and Quebec and the west. The -people in those states which have to contend with climatic conditions similar to those in Canada have to spend large sums of money in providing for their families and stock.
Where the figures are unsatisfactory the farmers have to cope with such climatic conditions as the farmers in Canada must contend against, while those states which show an increase in prosperity are in the south where there is no winter, where capital investment is not high, and where in many instances the farms produce two or three crops annually. In the southern states, in addition, there is the advantage of cheap labour as compared with what our farmers have to pay in this direction. The farmers of the south raise their crops under more favourable conditions and they invade the markets of the north. The twenty-four states in the north ought to be more prosperous from the standpoint of population, for I venture to say that 75 per cent of the population of the United States is located in this northern territory. Take the cities of Chicago, Buffalo, Detroit-they are all situated in that area. Yet the states in which those cities are located are going backwards. Why? As the member for South Huron pointed out-and he was correct in what he said-these farmers are not getting on so well as the farmers in Canada and the reason is that they are bound to submit to the competition of the farmers in the southern states, where there is a warm climate and where there is every advantage to aid them in competition.

Would the northern
farmers improve conditions by shutting out the southern agricultural products?

Yes, undoubtedly they would improve their condition if they could do so, but they cannot. They have to put up with that competition also, and that was the very point taken by the deputation of farmers representing the northern states who went to congress and said, "These are conditions which we are up against; you cannot protect us from the competition of our fellow farmers to the south, but you can give us protection against the farmers of
Canada and the other farmers of the world." That is what was back of the Fordney-Mc-Cumber tariff; that is why it was put in force, because the farmers in the northern states demanded that protection. Some one will say, "Oh well, the competition of the south does not amount to anything." It amounts to a great deal; it is not merely competition in early vegetables, either. The state of Texas ranks second in the number of sheep, and has over 6,000,000 head of cattle, while in Canada we have about 9,000,000. Texas and Oklahoma together have almost as many cattle as there are in Canada.

about the prices of such things, and there are lots of men who are not ministers who do not need to worry. But I would impress upon hon. gentlemen that the high cost of living is a matter which must be considered. Meat is dear at one cent per pound if you do not have the cent; the cost of an article depends upon the ability to pay, whether or not the price is high. It does not make any difference to a millionaire whether or not beefsteak is a dollar a pound, but it makes a difference to the ordinary man. Hon. gentlemen opposite want to get it into their heads that they must adopt a policy which will enable workmen in Canada to secure employment at a wage which will permit them to buy decent food and decent clothing.

Will the hon. gentleman
permit a question as a matter of information? To what does he attribute this sudden development of opposition on the part of the northern farmers to those of the south? They were there all the time, were they not.?

I. do not
think the word "sudden" is quite well placed there. I think it has been developing for years but it takes some time for people to leam wisdom; we have had that exemplified here, as my hon. friend must admit when he looks about him on the other side of the House. He must see how long it has taken hon. gentlemen over there, who are supposed to be intelligent, to really grasp these things; they do not seem to have time to study them and to get at the basic principles of economics. How much less then, should we find fault with ordinary people in the country to our south? But no matter whether the time was long or short it is indisputable that the Fordney-Mc-Cumber tariff was placed on the statute books of the United States because of the demand of the American farmers that they should have the American market for their produce, particularly as against the farmers of Canada. I say that is the policy of the party on this side of the House.
The hon. gentleman admits that the competition from the southern states is more serious than from Canada?

Let me tell my hon. friend this: If the reciprocity pact had gone into effect the farmers of Canada would have been up against competition from the south just as the farmers from the northern states were. We have a measure of protection but in my humble judgment it is not sufficient in many respects to give the farmer in this country the protection to which he is entitled. That is the point I make. I say that if the Liberal party had carried the 
reciprocity pact into effect and allowed the door to this country to be opened, then the farmers in Ontario who, according to the member for South Huron (Mr. McMillan) are more prosperous than those in New York and Pennsylvania, would be in the same position as the farmers in the northern states- they would be subjected to competition from the southern farmers who are raising their produce under more advantageous conditions than the farmers to the north.
Will the hon. member explain why the Fordney-McCumber tariff has not fulfilled its purpose, and has not given satisfaction?

My hon.
friend has asked me why the Fordney-McCumber tariff has not produced the results desired. I think you can find the reason for it in the volume of importations as compared with the amount produced on the other side of the line. Do not forget the fact that the people of the United States do not all live in cities. The United States is still a great farming country with an immense surplus of farm products. They are up against, and must continue to be up against, the competition of the farmers in the southern states who have a milder climate. You cannot give protection against the climate, but the farmers over there do enjoy a certain amount of protection. They certainly enjoy an amount of protection by reason of the duty imposed against Canadian products, there is no question at all about that. They must enjoy protection or they would not have asked for an increase in the tariff rates such as they asked for not very long since.

The hon. gentleman will admit that a duty of 42 cents a bushel on wheat does not raise the price of wheat in the United States for the simple reason that they have an exportable surplus. The hon. gentleman laughed a moment ago when I gave him that argument

That is all very well but I wonder why that explanation has not occurred to the statesmen of the United States. What did they put a duty of 42 cents on wheat, a duty of 12 cents a pound on butter, and a duty of 8 cents a dozen on eggs? Why do they do these things? Is it because the statesmen in the United States, as well as in Japan, Germany and every other country on the face of the earth -who are raising their tariffs, especially since the war, with the idea of protecting their people against depreciated foreign currencies and low rates of wages, and to make good

the loss of money which resulted in the war -have no intelligence; that the only persons who have intelligence are the gentlemen sitting on the treasury benches of Canada? This country is the only country in the world that I know of which, notwithstanding the economic and other changes which have taken place since the war, has lowered its tariS.
There are several other matters I should have liked to discuss for various reasons, but one reason has left the chamber-I refer to the Minister of Railways. There are a number of matters I should have liked to talk about, because I think there is room in that hon. gentleman's head for information. There are still some things he should know that he does not know, and that he particularly ought to know because he occupies an important position in the country. He is woefully deficient in the very elements of knowledge which he should possess as a minister of the crown.

Why not give him a few
private lessons?

I will do
that, but I will not say how many I will give him. It all depends, however, upon his acquisitiveness as a pupil. An hon. gentleman suggests that he should have these lessons as long as he lives. I suppose one would need to give him lessons for a long time in order to fill up the aching void in his brain?
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I submit this on behalf of the party of which I have the honour to be an humble member:	The Conservative party does not now and has not in the past advocated a high tariff which will exclude foreign competition. WTe do not believe in that and we never have believed in it. But we do believe in developing Canadian industries which will employ Canadian workmen. We do believe in a policy which will keep our boys and girls employed in Canada rather than drive them to the United States. That is the policy we believe in, and I think it is one which should engage the attention of every man in this House no matter with what party he is affiliated. Let us give employment to our own children within the bounds of Canada, let us build up this Dominion. We can only do that by creating living conditions in this country such as will induce our young folks to stay here. Let us give reasonable, just and fair protection and not one fraction of a cent more. Above all let us give the basic industry of agriculture what it has never had in my judgment under any party in Canada, a square deal amongst the industries so far as the tariff is concerned. That is all I have to say in regard to the matter.
I have some information here which I obtained in answer to questions of mine in regard to the importations of butter from Australia and New Zealand, but I will not take the time to go into that matter to-night. We shall have an opportunity perhaps to bring the subject up when we are in committee. I will simply say that the figures which have been given to me in answer to questions which I put on the order paper show conclusively and beyond any shadow of doubt the disastrous results to Canada which have followed the action of the government in making a treaty arrangement with Australia something over a year ago. I am sure the government is convinced of that, but it is proved by the figures in my possession.
